llmapi.q: What does the system prompt do in a chat API request?
options: It stores the conversation between calls on the server
It gives standing instructions such as role, rules and format
It sets the maximum number of output tokens
It selects which model version answers
llmapi.why: The system prompt carries instructions that apply to every turn. The model keeps no memory between calls, so history must be re-sent in messages.

llmapi.q: A response comes back with stop_reason set to max_tokens. What does that tell you?
options: The model refused to answer the question
The request used too many input tokens
The answer hit the output cap and was cut off
The rate limit was reached during generation
llmapi.why: max_tokens means generation stopped because it reached the output limit, so the answer is probably incomplete.

llmapi.q: Bramwell Foods needs invoice fields extracted into JSON the same way every time. Which setting fits best, if the model allows it?
options: A low temperature and a max_tokens that fits the JSON
A high temperature so the model explores more options
top_p of 1.0 and temperature of 1.0 together
A very small max_tokens to save money
llmapi.why: Extraction needs focused, repeatable output, so low temperature helps. Too small a max_tokens would cut off the JSON.

llmapi.q: A nightly job of 30,000 calls gets many 429 errors. What should you do first?
options: Retry every failed call immediately in a tight loop
Switch to a larger model with more capacity
Reduce concurrency and retry with backoff, respecting retry-after
Treat 429 like a 400 and fix the request body
llmapi.why: 429 means you exceeded a rate limit. Lower parallelism and backoff retries fix it; immediate retries make it worse.

llmapi.q: Spot the mistake: a team uses a floating model alias in production to 'always get the best model'. What is the risk?
options: Aliases cost twice as much as pinned ids
Aliases do not support streaming
Aliases only work through a gateway
The model can change underneath them and alter approved outputs
llmapi.why: An alias can move to a new version without any code change, so behaviour shifts silently. Pin an exact id and upgrade after running evals.

aicoding.q: Which task is a coding agent usually strongest at?
options: Deciding the customer's unwritten business rules
Writing tests for an existing, well-defined function
Choosing the system architecture on its own
Knowing the performance limits of a private database
aicoding.why: Tests for existing code have a clear target and are easy to check. Business rules and architecture need context the agent does not have.

aicoding.q: What is a project rules file such as CLAUDE.md for?
options: Giving the agent build commands, conventions and hard rules each session
Storing the API keys the agent needs to run
Logging every prompt sent to the model
Replacing the need for tests in the repository
aicoding.why: The rules file is read at the start of a session so the agent knows how to build, test and what not to touch. Secrets never belong in it.

aicoding.q: At Glenrock Energy you want an agent to debug a failing export. The folder holds a .env file and a customer data dump. What first?
options: Let the agent read everything so it has full context
Paste only the first 100 rows of the dump into the prompt
Move secrets and real data out, use a masked sample, then start
Ask the agent to promise not to read those files
aicoding.why: Agents read files in the working directory, so remove secrets and real personal data first and work from masked samples.

aicoding.q: You join a customer with a large unfamiliar codebase. How should you use an agent in the first days?
options: Ask it to rewrite the main module in a cleaner style
Give it production access so it can inspect live data
Skip reading code and rely on its summary alone
Ask read-only questions with file paths, then verify in the code
aicoding.why: Read-only mapping with cited paths is fast and checkable. Agent explanations can be wrong, so confirm them by opening the files.

aicoding.q: Spot the trap: the agent's change makes all tests pass. Which sign should worry you most?
options: It edited an existing test's expected value
It added a docstring to a new function
It kept the diff under 50 lines
It used a helper already present in the repo
aicoding.why: Changing a test to match the code can hide a real bug. Tests are the check, so edits to them need explicit review.
